name: Clear Cell Sarcoma of the Kidney

clinicalPearls: Second most common primary renal malignancy of childhood after Wilms tumour, with a peak in toddlers and preschool children and a male predominance.
Historically termed the bone-metastasising renal tumour of childhood — bone is the classic metastatic site, though brain, lung, liver and lymph nodes are also involved.

The recurrent molecular hallmark is an internal tandem duplication of BCOR (exon 15); a distinct minority harbour a YWHAE-NUTM2 gene fusion, and the two alterations are essentially mutually exclusive.

Histology is a great mimic with many patterns (classic, myxoid, sclerosing, cellular, epithelioid, palisading, spindle, storiform and anaplastic); the classic pattern shows nests and cords divided by a delicate chicken-wire capillary network, with pale cells and nuclear grooves.
Immunohistochemistry typically shows nuclear BCOR and cyclin D1 positivity and is negative for WT1, CD34 and epithelial or germ-cell markers, which helps separate it from Wilms tumour.
INI1/SMARCB1 expression is retained; its loss instead indicates malignant rhabdoid tumour of the kidney, the key differential to exclude.
Late relapses, notably in bone and brain, occur and mandate prolonged surveillance beyond the usual window applied to Wilms tumour.
Managed on renal-tumour protocols with nephrectomy, anthracycline-based chemotherapy and flank or abdominal radiotherapy, which have substantially improved survival.
reference.pathophysiology: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney is a paediatric renal sarcoma of uncertain histogenesis, thought to arise from primitive renal mesenchyme or stromal cells rather than from the nephrogenic (blastemal) epithelium of Wilms tumour. The defining and most frequent driver is an internal tandem duplication within exon 15 of BCOR (BCL6 corepressor), a component of a non-canonical polycomb repressive complex (PRC1.1) that regulates transcription and chromatin state; the duplication leads to BCOR overexpression and deregulated polycomb-mediated gene repression. A smaller subset is driven by the t(10;17) YWHAE-NUTM2 (formerly YWHAE-FAM22) gene fusion, and these two events are largely mutually exclusive. Both converge on transcriptional dysregulation that drives the neoplastic phenotype. The tumour is not linked to the WT1 pathway of Wilms tumour, consistent with its characteristically WT1-negative immunophenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant rhabdoid tumour of the kidney (SMARCB1/INI1 loss) — the critical distinction
Congenital mesoblastic nephroma, particularly the cellular type (ETV6-NTRK3)
Renal cell carcinoma, including translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma
Metanephric tumours, including metanephric stromal tumour
Ewing sarcoma / primitive neuroectodermal tumour of the kidney
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional abdominal imaging (ultrasound with contrast-enhanced CT or MRI) to characterise and stage the renal mass
Nephrectomy or biopsy histopathology with a panel of immunohistochemistry (BCOR, cyclin D1, WT1, INI1/SMARCB1)
Molecular testing for the BCOR internal tandem duplication and the YWHAE-NUTM2 fusion
Skeletal imaging and bone scintigraphy to detect bone metastases
Brain MRI given the tropism for central nervous system relapse
Chest CT to detect pulmonary metastases
Baseline cardiac assessment (echocardiography) before anthracycline-based therapy
redFlags: Palpable abdominal mass with haematuria or hypertension in a young child
New bone pain or a pathological fracture suggesting skeletal metastasis
Neurological symptoms suggesting brain relapse, even years after treatment
Tumour rupture or haemorrhage, or extension into the renal vein or inferior vena cava
reference.prognosis: Outcomes have improved markedly with combined nephrectomy, anthracycline-based chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and most localised cases are now curable. Higher stage, anaplasia and relapse — particularly late bone or brain recurrence — worsen the prognosis, so extended follow-up is essential.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the tumour as Wilms tumour or another small round or spindle cell renal tumour without molecular and immunohistochemical confirmation.
Failing to exclude malignant rhabdoid tumour by confirming that INI1/SMARCB1 expression is retained.
Curtailing surveillance too early and missing a late bone or brain relapse.
Attributing skeletal lesions to benign causes and delaying the metastatic work-up.
